summary: Defines a MIB module of textual conventions for representing common Internet network layer addresses, so other MIB modules can import them instead of defining their own.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4001 defines shared data types for recording Internet addresses in management information bases (MIBs). A type value tells a reader whether the address is Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4), version 6 (IPv6), a scoped address, or a Domain Name System (DNS) name.

subtitle: Shared MIB types for representing Internet addresses and related values.

tldr.problem: The SMIv2 IpAddress type represents only four-byte IPv4 addresses. MIB modules also need a common way to describe IPv6 addresses, names, zones, and prefixes.
tldr.mechanism: The INET-ADDRESS-MIB defines an address-type value alongside an address byte string. It also defines conventions for zones, prefix lengths, ports, autonomous system numbers, scopes, and IP versions.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4001 obsoletes RFC 3291 and recommends these shared types for new MIB definitions that represent Internet network addresses.

today: RFC 4001 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3291. The batch metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Shared Address Types Are Needed
sections.content:
The Structure of Management Information version 2 (SMIv2) IpAddress type can hold only a four-byte Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) address. RFC 4001 defines textual conventions that let management information bases (MIBs) describe Internet network addresses in a common, extensible way.

The conventions work with SMIv1 and SMIv2. New MIB definitions SHOULD use them rather than define their own address representations, and new MIB modules SHOULD NOT use IpAddress. Transport-layer addresses are outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The older address type can record only IPv4. This RFC gives MIB authors shared types that can describe IPv4, IPv6, and DNS names without inventing a new format for each module.

sections.title: The Address Type and Address Value
sections.content:
A generic address uses two objects: InetAddressType and InetAddress. The type says how to interpret the address value. Defined types include unknown(0), ipv4(1), ipv6(2), ipv4z(3), ipv6z(4), and dns(16).

InetAddress is an octet string with a size from 0 to 255 octets. The type and address must remain consistent. A management operation that changes one in a way that makes the other invalid must fail with inconsistentValue.
sections.plainLanguage: Each address has a companion type that explains how to read it. If a management system changes an address from one format to another, it must update the type and value consistently.

sections.title: Address Forms, Zones, and Prefixes
sections.content:
The module defines concrete conventions for IPv4 addresses (4 octets), IPv6 addresses (16 octets), zoned IPv4 addresses (8 octets), zoned IPv6 addresses (20 octets), and DNS names (1 to 255 octets). A zone index distinguishes the same non-global address used on different zones; zero identifies a default zone.

InetAddressPrefixLength represents a network prefix length from 0 to 2040. Its interpretation depends on the address type: values above the address maximum are treated as that maximum. The maximum is 32 for IPv4 types, 128 for IPv6 types, and 0 for DNS names.
sections.plainLanguage: Some addresses need an extra zone number to identify the right network interface. A prefix length says how much of an address identifies its network, and its meaning depends on the address type.

sections.title: Using the Conventions in MIB Tables
sections.content:
Every use of InetAddress or InetAddressPrefixLength must identify the related InetAddressType. When a generic address indexes a table, both the type and address are required, in that order, and the IMPLIED keyword must not be used for the address.

A MIB description must explain when and how a DNS name is resolved if communication needs its IP address. It must also explain which address is reported when a host has multiple addresses or names.
sections.plainLanguage: When a table stores a general address, it must also identify the address type that explains it. MIB authors must document how DNS names are resolved and which address is reported when several are available.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
This module defines textual conventions, not management objects. RFC 4001 says meaningful security considerations belong in the MIB modules that define and use the managed objects.

The module is registered as part of the INET-ADDRESS-MIB under mib-2 76. RFC 4001 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 3291.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC defines data types rather than objects that manage a system, so it leaves security analysis to the MIBs that use those types. It replaces RFC 3291 as the address-convention document.
